[MUQATIL:50:3/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The deniers say that returning to life after death and becoming dust is far-fetched, denying that resurrection will happen.
[MUQATIL:50:3/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The verse was revealed about Quraysh deniers Abu ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Ashaddayn (Usayda ibn Kalda), and the brothers Nabh and Munabbih, sons of al-Hajjaj; they asked how God could revive them once they were dust scattered in the earth.
[FARRA:v3p75/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The question’s lead-in is omitted: the oath implies You will surely be raised after death; the disbelievers reject this and call resurrection a far-fetched return.
[FARRA:v3p75/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | They deny resurrection outright; بعيد can describe someone far from the truth, as when a person errs in an answer.
[MAJAZ:v2p222/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The phrase means a far-fetched return or restoration.
[AKHFASH:v2p522/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The phrase omits an explicit statement that resurrection is occurring because it answers an assertion that they will return: they object that return after becoming dust is remote.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p417#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The deniers mean that resurrection after death will not happen.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p141/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | An oath may omit its answer when later words make it clear; here the implied answer is that the dead will be resurrected, which the disbelievers deny. | mentions 79:1, 79:6
[ZAJJAJ:v5p41/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The question means “shall we be raised when we have died and become dust?”; idhā must connect to a verb for the statement to have a point.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p42/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The deniers call resurrection a remote return because they consider it far-fetched after death.
[NAHHAS:v4p219/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The objection asks whether they will be resurrected after dying and becoming dust; al-Farra says baʿīd here means it will not happen, a recognized Arabic usage.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p281/r7] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | reports | Yahya, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abu Jaʿfar, and Safwan ibn ʿAmr read "إذا متنا" without an interrogative hamza.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p281/r8] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | rejects | One explanation supplies a deleted interrogative hamza from the common reading, but Ibn Jinnī recalls having judged this deletion explanation weak.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p281/r9] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | Alternatively, the reading is non-interrogative: after death and becoming dust, they would be brought back; "distant return" means implausible to them, not far off in time, since they denied resurrection altogether.
[THALABI:v9p93/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The question means, “Will we be raised after we die and become dust?” The mention of resurrection is elided because the context makes it clear.
[THALABI:v9p93/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | They call resurrection a far-fetched return; the commentary gives the verb's forms as rajʿan and rujuʿan and cites its Quranic usage. | mentions 9:83
[QUSHAYRI:v3p225/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | One proposed, omitted response to the oath is that they will indeed be raised at the Resurrection.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p225/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The unbelievers deny resurrection and deem it far-fetched that they could be raised after dying and becoming dust.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p377/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says the response is omitted and indicated by the question at 50:3: the oath means they will surely be resurrected, which they deny; al-Zajjaj also chooses this reading. | mentions 50:3
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p379#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi explains rajʿ as a return or reversal, citing the verb in 9:83. | mentions 9:83
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:50:1-4/r5] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Their question about being raised after death and becoming dust is an interrogative denial with an omitted answer.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:50:1-4/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They then outright deny resurrection, calling it an impossible return.
[DAMGHANI:v1p86/r2] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | تراب in the question about being raised again means decayed remains. | mentions 50:3
[JISHUMI:v9p6545/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبي | reports | Ubayy reports that the Prophet said whoever recites Sūrat Qāf will have death's agonies eased; no grading is stated.
[JISHUMI:v9p6545/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Qāf opens with resurrection, the Qurʾān, and proofs of God's oneness, following al-Ḥujurāt's close on faith and its conditions.
[JISHUMI:v9p6545/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Marjiʿ is the verbal noun of rajaʿa, return.
[JISHUMI:v9p6550/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Rationally, resurrection concerns those entitled to reward or compensation; revelation says all living beings will be restored.
[JISHUMI:v9p6550/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Resurrection is demonstrated by God's power over bodies and His knowledge of their parts.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p356/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The question omits “will we be raised?” because context makes resurrection understood; they call return to life far-fetched and impossible.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r10] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Alternatively rajʿ means the returned answer, making this God’s comment that their denial of resurrection is itself outlandish.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r11] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A reading has idhā in declarative form rather than a question; it is understood as when we die after we have returned, as the following phrase indicates.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r12] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | If rajʿ means the returned answer, the time adverb is governed by the resurrection matter implied by the word warner.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Their denial of resurrection is especially absurd: they acknowledge God’s power to originate all things, admit the first creation, and reason requires recompense.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | He replaces the pronoun with disbelievers to mark the gravity of their unbelief, focusing on their rejection of resurrection.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | That points to the return to life after death.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The time adverb is governed by an implied verb: will we be returned when we have died and decayed?
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p383#2/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Far means beyond customary experience and what the mind considers plausible.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p156/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinni allows the sense: when we die, are we then returned? ذلك رجع بعيد supplies the predicate and answer.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p156/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Raj is the verbal noun of raja'tuhu, to return something.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p156/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The alleged remoteness of resurrection is its supposed impossibility in people's minds and thoughts.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p156/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | God knows what the earth consumes of Adam's descendants and preserves it in a record, so their return is fully known.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p156/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الأعرج وشيبة وأبو جعفر | reports | Al-Araj, Shayba, and Abu Jaafar read إذا declaratively, without the interrogative hamza; رجع بعيد is its predicate.
[TABRISI:50:1-5/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The disbelievers called Muhammad's message astonishing because they denied both a messenger from their own people and resurrection after death.
[TABRISI:50:1-5/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They deem return to life far beyond imagination and impossible, so they deny that it can occur.
[TABRISI:50:1-5/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The governing verb for “when we die” is implicit: the intended question is whether they will be resurrected after death.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p6#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash reads the question as a response to an implied statement: “You will be returned,” followed by their objection about being dead and dust.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p6#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Another parse supplies an oath by Qaf and the Quran that they will be raised, followed by the question about being dead and dust.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p6#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن جرير | reports | Ibn Jarir links their astonishment at God's warning for denying Muhammad to their claim that resurrection is strange: they were told they would learn the outcome when raised.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p6#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Raj' means return to life.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p6#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba says “far-fetched” means that it will not happen.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p125/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī says Sūrat Qāf is recited in Eid prayer: Eid's festivity should remind worshippers of the gathering for judgment and deter heedlessness and sin; the sūra's Quranic reminder suits the day. | mentions 50:42, 50:11, 50:44, 50:45
[RAZI-FULL:v28p125/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Sūrat Qāf and Sūrat Ṣād share openings with an isolated letter, an oath by the Quran, “bal,” and an expression of wonder; each also opens and closes with a reminder about the Quran. | mentions 38:1, 38:87, 50:45
[RAZI-FULL:v28p125/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ṣād foregrounds the first principle, God's unity, while Qāf foregrounds resurrection; Ṣād ends by recalling Adam's creation as proof of unity, and Qāf ends with the gathering. | mentions 38:5, 3

[RAZI-FULL:v28p130#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī says “this is a strange thing” is a second expression of wonder, about resurrection and the warner's warning of it.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p130#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In Ṣād, “indeed this is astonishing” follows the challenge to make one God, whereas in Qāf the phrase follows the warner's arrival and precedes the separate objection to resurrection. | mentions 38:5
[RAZI-FULL:v28p130#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “That return is far” already expresses wonder at resurrection, so assigning “this is strange” to resurrection would repeat it; instead it confirms their wonder at the messenger after God rebukes misplaced amazement. | mentions 11:73
[RAZI-FULL:v28p130#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī also distinguishes the near “this” from the distant “that”: the first points to the present arrival of the warner, the second to the future return.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p131#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī links the opponents' astonishment at the messenger to their dismissal of his message, citing their accusations that he would turn people from ancestral worship and that his message was fabricated. | mentions 34:43
[RAZI-FULL:v28p131#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Their question is an explicit or implied denial prompted by the warner: warning of lasting punishment entails resurrection.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p131#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “That” points to the warned-of return, while “this is strange” points to the messenger's arrival; the messenger is present but the warned-of event is distant.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p131#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Rāzī explains rajʿ as a verbal noun usable with a transitive sense; rujuʿ and al-rujʿā are intransitive verbal nouns, and rajʿ can also be intransitive. | mentions 96:8
[RAZI-FULL:v28p131#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The phrase can mean a far-off return, supported by 96:8, or a far-off raising, supported by 79:10; on the transitive reading they deny that resurrection is possible. | mentions 96:8, 79:10
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:1-4/r21] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The disbelievers' question has an omitted predicate: will we be raised after dying and becoming dust?
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:1-4/r22] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rajaʿ means return; they call resurrection a remote return, meaning impossible.
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:1-4/r23] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A second ellipsis supplies their repeated objection: they said, “Will we be resurrected when we die?”
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:1-4/r24] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Resurrection need not have been mentioned immediately before: it occurs elsewhere, the Qur'an is like one surah, and a warner's warning entails afterlife punishment and judgment.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:50:3-5/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The implied question is whether they return after dying and becoming dust, as the following phrase shows.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:50:3-5/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The return seems remote from imagination, customary experience, or possibility; الرجع may instead mean the returned thing.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their question expresses astonishment and intensifies the claim that resurrection is unlikely and deserves denial.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Calling them the disbelievers instead of using a pronoun marks the gravity of the unbelief in their statement.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Dhālika points to resurrection.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · نافع وعلى وحمزة وحفص | reports | Nāfiʿ, ʿAlī, Ḥamza, and Ḥafṣ read mitnā with the vowel form recorded in the commentary.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Baʿīd means judged far-fetched and rejected, remote from imagination and ordinary experience, as in saying this is a distant statement.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p170/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Alternatively, al-rajʿ means return or response and the words are God's characterization of their denial of the promised resurrection; on this reading a pause after turāban is good, with the time adverb governed by the warning of resurrection.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p526#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | حَادَ عن الشيء means to turn away or incline from it; he gives the verbal nouns حيودا، حيدة، and حيدودة.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p529/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأعرج وشيبة وأبو جعفر وابن وثاب والأعمش وابن عتبة | reports | These readers pronounce إذا with one hamza as a declarative form; it may conceal an interrogative hamza or state their claim that they will return after becoming dust.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p529/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | With the interrogative reading, the time expression depends on an omitted verb meaning 'Will we be raised when we die?'; 'that' points to resurrection, which they deem remote.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p529/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī allows رجع to mean 'the returned thing' and to be God's own expression of their rejection; Abū Ḥayyān calls this interpretation astonishing and unintelligible to Arabs.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · العامة | reports | The common reading has two hamzas and is interrogative. Ibn ʿĀmir in one transmission, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash, and al-Aʿraj use one hamza, possibly interrogative with the particle omitted or declarative.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | In the common interrogative reading, an implicit verb such as أنبعث or أنرجع governs إذا.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | With the declarative reading, the answer after إذا is omitted: “we returned.”
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قيل | reports | Some take ذلك رجع as the answer to إذا with the fāʾ deleted; the majority disallow this except in poetry.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī reads الرجع as “the thing returned” (resurrection), a divine answer exposing the deniers’ rejection; on this parse, stop before it.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | On al-Zamakhsharī’s parse, the adverb is governed by what “the warned” implies, namely the warning about resurrection.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The Shaykh sharply criticizes al-Zamakhsharī for understanding the passage this way.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p394#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | prefers | Ibn Kathir prefers the implicit answer in the ensuing message: establishing prophethood and resurrection; Qur'anic oaths often work this way, as in another sura. | mentions 38:1, 38:2
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p394#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | They ask how they can return to their former bodily form after death, decay, severed limbs, and becoming dust; they regard resurrection as impossible.
[BURHAN:v3p333/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن الزبير | reports | Ibn al-Zubayr treats Qaf's move from denial of resurrection to visible signs in the sky and revived land as a comparable shift; these undeniable signs lead to the conclusion that resurrection will likewise occur. | mentions 50:1, 50:6, 50:9
[BURHAN:v3p333/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | After leaving the disbelievers' challenge unanswered and describing the heavens and rain as observable facts they could not deny, God concludes: “Thus is the emergence.” | mentions 50:6, 50:9
[BURHAN:v3p81/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | من is added after negation or its equivalent for emphasis, as in verses about a falling leaf, creation, and God's having a child or partner. | mentions 50:3, 6:100
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p246/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Their denial does not stem from rejecting the Qurʾān's glory or the Prophet's truth; rather, the unbelievers are astonished.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p246/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Their objection imagines their souls separated from their bodies at death and their bodies reduced to dust indistinguishable from the earth's soil.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p246/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Their reasoning is inconsistent: they marvel at a human messenger and being returned from dust, yet accept stone gods and do not marvel that they first came to life from dust.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p246/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The regular return of day and night, revival of dead land, first life in animals, and emergence of plants, trees, and fruit all make resurrection evident rather than strange.
[DURR-FULL:v7p589/r1] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says the deniers rejected resurrection, asking who could restore them to life.
[BURSEVI:v9p82#3/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | They ask whether, after dying, their souls separate from bodies and they become indistinguishable from earth, they will be returned and raised despite the great difference from their former living state; the interrogative rejects resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The opening reports their astonishment, intensifies their denial, or identifies the point they find astonishing.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If read declaratively, the answer is omitted: when we die and become dust, we shall return.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صاحب اللوامح | reports | The author of al-Lawami permits ذلك رجع بعيد as the conditional answer after deletion of فاء; grammarians otherwise allow this only in poetic necessity.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The governing word for إذا is omitted but obvious: when we die and become dust, will we return, despite the change from life to death?
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | ذلك points to the disputed return,

 resurrection after death.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | They call the return remote from imagination, ordinary experience, or possibility.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غير مسمى | reports | An alternative takes رجع as a response or reply, as in “this is the reply to your letter”; ذلك then points back to their question.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غير مسمى | reports | On the reply reading, the sentence is God's speech describing their answer to the warner as far-fetched; إذا is governed by the warned-of resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The objection that the reply reading leaves إذا without a governor fails: their answer itself shows they had been warned of resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi considers رجع meaning “reply” remote; Abu Hayyan calls it a strange meaning beyond Arab comprehension.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p172#4/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأعرج، شيبة، أبو جعفر، ابن وثاب، الأعمش، ابن عتبة عن ابن عامر | reports | These readers use one hamza in إذا, resembling an indicative form; it may be an interrogative with its hamza omitted or a declarative.
[ELMALILI:50:1-5#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | On one reading, the next clause explains their amazement and makes their disbelief explicit: the particle fa is explanatory and “this” points to the Prophet’s warning.
[ELMALILI:50:1-5#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | On the other reading, after marveling at the Prophet’s mission they also marvel at resurrection: fa coordinates the clauses, and “this” refers ambiguously to their question about being raised after death.
[ELMALILI:50:1-5#3/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The phrase calls resurrection after death a distant return, remote from reason or custom; “ircāʿ” can also mean a reply or response.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p279/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This points to the situation in which the Prophet calls them to believe in resurrection, which the next verse spells out. | mentions 50:3
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p279/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Their question expresses astonishment and rejection, meant to make listeners regard resurrection as impossible; they base their wonder on the timing after death and bodily decay.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p279/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The questioned predicate is omitted after idhā: the implied question is whether they will return to life after death and reduction to dust, which they consider maximally inconceivable.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p279/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The declarative statement repeats and confirms the question directly, after its meaning was conveyed indirectly by ellipsis; explicit confirmation is clearer.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p279/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rujʿ is the verbal noun for returning to life; baʿīd means beyond rational conception, hence impossible.
[TABATABAI:50:1-4/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The sūrah warns of Resurrection and explains the polytheists' astonishment: death reduces identity to dust without trace, so they wonder how people return; God's encompassing knowledge and Preserved Book answer them, and past nations' destruction warns them.
[TABATABAI:50:1-4/r14] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | ‘Rather’ diverts from the omitted oath response: either they marvel that a warner came from among them, or they marvel at the true Resurrection they were warned of. | mentions 50:1, 50:2, 50:3
[TABATABAI:50:1-4/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Resurrection is the sūrah's focus; the author highlights the unveiling at 50:22, Hell's response at 50:30, and the Garden's abundance at 50:35. | mentions 50:22, 50:30, 50:35
[TABATABAI:50:1-4/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The sūrah is Meccan by its context; claims that the verse or verses about creation of heavens and earth are exceptions have no textual evidence.
